title: The Five Most Momentous Legal Tech Fails
author: Robert Ambrogi

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source documents failures of legal-technology products caused by performance, adoption and market difficulties, but it does not address AI’s jagged capabilities, verification, human expertise or work redesign. Its evidence is therefore only indirectly relevant to the cluster’s proposition and does not establish a clear position on it.
qs: Unfortunately, the product got off to a rocky start, with major performance issues, and it had difficulty gaining traction in what was fast becoming a crowded market.

By January 2017, LexisNexis said it was [discontinuing sales of Firm Manager](https://www.lawnext.com/2017/01/breaking-lexisnexis-discontinue-sales-firm-manager-practice-management-platform.html), and, later that year, it [shut it down entirely](https://www.lawnext.com/2017/05/lexisnexis-firm-manager-will-go-dark-oct-31-2017.html).

st.t: Atrium failure: Workflow automation could not secure viability
st.an: Ambrogi supports the cluster’s core caution that Atrium’s prominent founder, substantial funding and attempted pivot did not secure commercial survival. He also raises structural doubts by comparing Atrium with Clearspire, but offers no causal evidence sufficient to turn that parallel into proof that integrated legal-delivery models generally cannot succeed.
qs: It came out of the gate with $10 million in funding, and then a year later raised a whopping $65 million more from some of the biggest names in venture capital.

When it launched, I questioned in an [Above the Law](https://abovethelaw.com/2017/09/is-revolutionary-law-firm-atrium-a-case-of-clearspire-deja-vu/) column whether it was a case of Clearspire déjà vu, recalling the demise of the strikingly similar dual-entity firm Clearspire, which opened in 2010 and shut down four years later.

st.t: ROSS shutdown: Litigation can eliminate unresolved competitors
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition by attributing ROSS’s shutdown to the lawsuit’s impairment of financing and acquisition opportunities while treating the underlying allegations as disputed. It also confirms that operations ended before the litigation was resolved and that insurance funded the continuing defense and counterclaims.
qs: While ROSS vehemently denied the allegations, the lawsuit crippled its ability to raise new financing or explore potential acquisition opportunities.
Yet even though the company is no longer operating, it continues to fight the lawsuit, with its defense and counterclaims funded by insurance coverage.

kp.k: Legal technology innovation does not guarantee commercial survival
kp.d: Ambrogi presents five retrospective cases of legal technology failures over the preceding 10 years, qualifying enthusiasm about new products with examples of business closures. These are historical case accounts, not a systematic study of failure rates or predictions about AI adoption.
qs: While the last few years have brought an abundance of new and innovative legal tech products to market, the fact of the matter is that not every new product will succeed.
Let’s revisit five of the most momentous legal tech fails of the last 10 years.

kp.k: Atrium's funded dual-entity model failed within three years
kp.d: Atrium launched in 2017 combining a law firm and technology company, initially raising $10 million and another $65 million a year later. Ambrogi reports that it shut down within three years after attempting a business-model pivot. He compares its trajectory with Clearspire, another dual-entity firm that opened in 2010 and closed four years later, without establishing a specific cause of either failure.
qs: It launched in 2017 to great fanfare, promising to “revolutionize legal services” through its dual-entity model of both a law firm and a technology company.
It came out of the gate with $10 million in funding, and then a year later raised a whopping $65 million more from some of the biggest names in venture capital.
within three years, Atrium shut down, after first trying to pivot to a different business model.

kp.k: QuickLegal closed following reporting on founder misconduct allegations
kp.d: Ambrogi describes Derek Bluford's ventures in consumer legal services, on-demand legal advice and cloud practice management. He reports that QuickLegal closed after his 2016 reporting on a lawsuit settlement involving allegations of lawyer impersonation, forged legal documents and client fraud. LawTova and another linked startup subsequently closed after further reporting. Separately from those allegations and the settlement, the article reports Bluford's 2021 sentence of seven years in prison on related charges.
qs: But that all came crashing down after I reported in 2016 of Bluford’s settlement of a lawsuit charging him with impersonating a lawyer, forging legal documents and fraudulently swindling two clients.
Following my report, QuickLegal quickly shut down.
Then, in 2021, he was sentenced to seven years in prison on charges related to the fraud and forgeries I’d written about in 2016.

kp.k: ROSS pioneered AI research but litigation constrained its financing
kp.d: ROSS began in 2014 as a University of Toronto student entry in an IBM Watson competition and attracted investors including Denton's NextLaw Labs. Ambrogi characterizes it as an early AI legal-research venture. He attributes its December 2020 shutdown to financing and acquisition constraints following Thomson Reuters' 2020 lawsuit alleging appropriation of Westlaw content. ROSS denied the allegations; the article does not report an adjudicated finding and states that the litigation remained ongoing at writing, with insurance funding its defense and counterclaims.
qs: ROSS was ahead of its time in striving to use artificial intelligence to empower legal research.
It started in 2014 at the University of Toronto as a student-built entrant in a cognitive-computing competition staged by IBM to develop applications for its Watson computer.
While ROSS vehemently denied the allegations, the lawsuit crippled its ability to raise new financing or explore potential acquisition opportunities.
Yet even though the company is no longer operating, it continues to fight the lawsuit, with its defense and counterclaims funded by insurance coverage.
As of this writing, the lawsuit is ongoing.

kp.k: Firm Manager's redesign did not reverse its commercial difficulties
kp.d: LexisNexis entered cloud practice management for smaller firms in 2011, following Clio and Rocket Matter in 2008 and MyCase in 2009. Ambrogi reports major early performance problems and difficulty gaining traction in an increasingly crowded market. A near-complete rebuild produced Firm Manager 2.0 in 2016, but LexisNexis discontinued sales in January 2017 and closed the product later that year.
qs: Unfortunately, the product got off to a rocky start, with major performance issues, and it had difficulty gaining traction in what was fast becoming a crowded market.
It later went back to the drawing board and rebuilt the product almost from the ground up, releasing the retooled version in 2016 as Firm Manager 2.0.

kp.k: Gavelytics' platform and data survived through acquisition
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that litigation analytics provider Gavelytics, founded in California in 2017, expanded its product and raised funding before unexpectedly closing in 2022. On June 29, 2022, founder Rick Merrill notified customers and employees of closure the following day. The article supplies no specific cause of failure. Six months later, Pre/Dicta acquired the platform and accumulated court data and retained Merrill as a strategic advisor.
qs: When the litigation analytics company Gavelytics shut down in 2022, it was a shock to almost everybody but the founder.
Six months after it shut down, another litigation analytics startup, Pre/Dicta,
and its accumulated court data, and brought on Merrill as a strategic advisor.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ambrogi describes ROSS as an early attempt to empower legal research with AI, whose commercial survival was undermined by litigation rather than a reported failure of AI performance.
pts.d: Ambrogi characterises ROSS as ahead of its time in pursuing AI-assisted legal research. He reports that Thomson Reuters' 2020 lawsuit alleging misuse of Westlaw content crippled ROSS's financing and acquisition prospects, leading to its shutdown. The allegations are presented as disputed, not established facts. The article offers no quantified claim about AI's effect on research quality, productivity, staffing or prices, and no general prediction about AI replacing lawyers. The other failures concern legal technology or business models without an explicit AI-change claim.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a journalistic case history supported by Ambrogi's prior reporting, not measured AI performance.
pts.d: Ambrogi recounts ROSS's origins in a 2014 IBM cognitive-computing competition, investor interest, startup-incubator participation, his 2019 visit to its research and development office, and the subsequent lawsuit and shutdown. His linked reporting supplies the case-based foundation for the account. Investor attention and institutional recognition are indicators of commercial interest, not benchmarks demonstrating that AI improved legal research.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account covers ROSS's development from 2014 through its December 2020 shutdown announcement, with litigation continuing at the time of writing.
pts.d: The source's AI-related claim is retrospective rather than a forecast. The commercial constraint it identifies is the effect of a contested lawsuit on access to financing and potential acquirers. Ambrogi distinguishes the cessation of company operations from the continuation of litigation, which he says was supported by insurance coverage.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected market participant is an AI legal-research vendor, with implications for competition in legal research.
pts.d: Ambrogi reports the loss of ROSS as an operating provider and its inability to pursue new financing or acquisition opportunities. Thomson Reuters/Westlaw appears as the incumbent research provider alleging that ROSS used its content to build a competing product. Legal researchers are the intended beneficiaries of ROSS's AI ambition, but the article does not document specific effects on their work or clients. ROSS is described as a product company, not an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work.
